claim: Alexander disease (AxD) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder caused by mutations in glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP).
source: Alexander disease (AxD) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder caused by mutations in glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), which supports the structural integrity of astrocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to established literature in the introduction (Brenner et al., 2001).

claim: Over 70 GFAP missense mutations cause AxD.
source: Over 70 GFAP missense mutations cause AxD, but the mechanism linking different mutations to disease-relevant phenotypes remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and introduction, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Phosphorylation of GFAP-Ser13 is selectively present in AxD patients who died young, independently of the mutation they carried.
source: Our findings reveal selective phosphorylation of GFAP-Ser13 in patients who died young, independently of the mutation they carried.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 2A) and western blot validation (Figure 2B-C) from patient brain tissue.

claim: AxD iPSC-astrocytes accumulated pSer13-GFAP in cytoplasmic aggregates within deep nuclear invaginations.
source: AxD iPSC-astrocytes accumulated pSer13-GFAP in cytoplasmic aggregates within deep nuclear invaginations, resembling the hallmark Rosenthal fibers observed in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 6A) and electron microscopy (Figure 6B) of iPSC-astrocytes.

claim: Ser13 phosphorylation facilitated GFAP aggregation.
source: Ser13 phosphorylation facilitated GFAP aggregation and was associated with increased GFAP proteolysis by caspase-6.
evidence: This is supported by cell transfection experiments showing S13D and S13E phospho-mimic mutants form aggregates (Figure 3A-B).

claim: Ser13 phosphorylation was associated with increased GFAP proteolysis by caspase-6.
source: Ser13 phosphorylation facilitated GFAP aggregation and was associated with increased GFAP proteolysis by caspase-6.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing increased cleaved GFAP in S13D mutants (Figure 7A-B) and reduction with caspase-6 inhibitor (Figure 7C-D).

claim: Caspase-6 was selectively expressed in young AxD patients.
source: Furthermore, caspase-6 was selectively expressed in young AxD patients, and correlated with the presence of cleaved GFAP.
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis of patient brain tissue showing caspase-6 expression in young but not old patients (Figure 9A-C).

claim: Caspase-6 expression correlated with the presence of cleaved GFAP in AxD patients.
source: Furthermore, caspase-6 was selectively expressed in young AxD patients, and correlated with the presence of cleaved GFAP.
evidence: This is supported by western blot (Figure 9D-E) and immunofluorescence (Figure 9F) showing cleaved GFAP in young patients with caspase-6 expression.

claim: GFAP is the major component of the intermediate filament (IF) cytoskeleton in astrocytes.
source: GFAP is the major component of the intermediate filament (IF) cytoskeleton in astrocytes (Hol and Pekny, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to established literature.

claim: The accumulation and incorporation of mutant GFAP within cytoplasmic aggregates called Rosenthal fibers (RFs) causes reactive gliosis.
source: The accumulation and incorporation of mutant GFAP within cytoplasmic aggregates called Rosenthal fibers (RFs), causes reactive gliosis, leading to secondary injury to neurons and non-neuronal cells (Olabarria and Goldman, 2017; Wang et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018; Jones et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to supporting literature.

claim: Silencing GFAP via antisense oligonucleotide intervention in vivo eliminates RFs in a mouse model of AxD.
source: Silencing GFAP via antisense oligonucleotide intervention in vivo eliminates RFs, reverses the stress responses in astrocytes and other cell types, and improves the clinical phenotype in a mouse model of AxD (Hagemann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a specific study.

claim: Silencing GFAP via antisense oligonucleotide intervention reverses stress responses in astrocytes and other cell types in a mouse model of AxD.
source: Silencing GFAP via antisense oligonucleotide intervention in vivo eliminates RFs, reverses the stress responses in astrocytes and other cell types, and improves the clinical phenotype in a mouse model of AxD (Hagemann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a specific study.

claim: Silencing GFAP via antisense oligonucleotide intervention improves the clinical phenotype in a mouse model of AxD.
source: Silencing GFAP via antisense oligonucleotide intervention in vivo eliminates RFs, reverses the stress responses in astrocytes and other cell types, and improves the clinical phenotype in a mouse model of AxD (Hagemann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a specific study.

claim: Dysfunctional IFs directly cause or predispose to over 70 tissue-specific or systemic diseases.
source: In contrast, dysfunctional IFs directly cause or predispose to over 70 tissue-specific or systemic diseases, including neuropathies, myopathies, skin fragility, metabolic dysfunctions, and premature aging (Omary, 2009; www.interfil.org).
evidence: This is stated with citation to established literature and a database.

claim: Disease-associated IF proteins share abnormal post-translational modifications (PTMs) as a key molecular feature.
source: Disease-associated IF proteins share two key molecular features: abnormal post-translational modifications (PTMs) (Snider and Omary, 2014) and pathologic aggregation.
evidence: This is stated with citation to a review article.

claim: Disease-associated IF proteins share pathologic aggregation as a key molecular feature.
source: Disease-associated IF proteins share two key molecular features: abnormal post-translational modifications (PTMs) (Snider and Omary, 2014) and pathologic aggregation.
evidence: This is stated with citation to a review article.

claim: GFAP contains three functional domains: amino-terminal 'head' domain, central α-helical 'rod' domain and carboxy-terminal 'tail' domain.
source: Like all IF proteins, GFAP contains three functional domains: amino-terminal 'head' domain, central α-helical 'rod' domain and carboxy-terminal 'tail' domain (Eriksson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation to established literature.

claim: The globular head domain is essential for IF assembly and disassembly.
source: The globular head domain is essential for IF assembly and disassembly, which are regulated by various PTMs, in particular phosphorylation (Omary et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a review article.

claim: Phosphorylation of multiple sites in the head domain of GFAP (Thr-7, Ser-8, Ser-13, Ser-17 and Ser-34) regulates filament disassembly during mitosis.
source: It was shown previously that phosphorylation of multiple sites in the head domain of GFAP (Thr-7, Ser-8, Ser-13, Ser-17 and Ser-34) regulates filament disassembly during mitosis and GFAP turnover in non-mitotic cells (Inagaki et al., 1990; Takemura et al., 2002a; Inagaki et al., 1994; Inagaki et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Phosphorylation of multiple sites in the head domain of GFAP regulates GFAP turnover in non-mitotic cells.
source: It was shown previously that phosphorylation of multiple sites in the head domain of GFAP (Thr-7, Ser-8, Ser-13, Ser-17 and Ser-34) regulates filament disassembly during mitosis and GFAP turnover in non-mitotic cells (Inagaki et al., 1990; Takemura et al., 2002a; Inagaki et al., 1994; Inagaki et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Phosphorylation of GFAP has been observed after various injuries of the central nervous system (CNS) including kainic acid-induced seizures, cold-injury, and hypoxic-ischemic models.
source: Additionally, phosphorylation of GFAP has been observed after various injuries of the central nervous system (CNS) including kainic acid-induced seizures, cold-injury, and hypoxic-ischemic models, where phosphorylated GFAP is expressed in reactive astrocytes (Valentim et al., 1999; Takemura et al., 2002b; Sullivan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Phosphorylated GFAP is expressed in reactive astrocytes after CNS injury.
source: Additionally, phosphorylation of GFAP has been observed after various injuries of the central nervous system (CNS) including kainic acid-induced seizures, cold-injury, and hypoxic-ischemic models, where phosphorylated GFAP is expressed in reactive astrocytes (Valentim et al., 1999; Takemura et al., 2002b; Sullivan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Phosphorylation of GFAP is important for re-organization of the astrocyte IF cytoskeleton and plasticity in response to injury.
source: These observations reveal that phosphorylation of GFAP is important for re-organization of the astrocyte IF cytoskeleton and plasticity in response to injury.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited observations about GFAP phosphorylation after CNS injury.

claim: 12 unique phosphorylation sites on GFAP were identified in AxD patient brain tissue by phospho-proteomic analysis.
source: GFAP from the insoluble high salt extracts (HSEs), prepared according to the procedure described in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, was used in phospho-proteomic analysis, revealing 12 unique phosphorylation sites on GFAP in AxD (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The most abundantly phosphorylated residue on GFAP in AxD was Ser13 in the head domain.
source: While the AxD-specific phospho-peptides localized to all three functional domains of GFAP (head, rod, tail), the most abundantly phosphorylated residue was a conserved serine (Ser13) in the head domain (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ser13 on GFAP is conserved in human, rat and mouse.
source: While the AxD-specific phospho-peptides localized to all three functional domains of GFAP (head, rod, tail), the most abundantly phosphorylated residue was a conserved serine (Ser13) in the head domain (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is shown in the amino acid alignment in Figure 1D.

claim: The pSer13-GFAP peptide was selectively elevated in the cortex tissue from AxD patients who died very young (median age at death = 1.7 years; range 0.5–14 years).
source: Strikingly, we found that the pSer13-GFAP peptide was selectively elevated in the cortex tissue from AxD patients who died very young (median age at death = 1.7 years; range 0.5–14 years) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry quantification shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Significant phosphorylation of GFAP was not observed in control subjects.
source: Overall, we did not observe significant phosphorylation of GFAP in the control subjects (Figure 2—source data 1), or in AxD patients who lived 27–50 years (median age at death = 38 years).
evidence: This is stated based on mass spectrometry data.

claim: Significant phosphorylation of GFAP was not observed in AxD patients who lived 27–50 years.
source: Overall, we did not observe significant phosphorylation of GFAP in the control subjects (Figure 2—source data 1), or in AxD patients who lived 27–50 years (median age at death = 38 years).
evidence: This is stated based on mass spectrometry data.

claim: Immunoblot analysis using a phospho-specific antibody (KT13) against pSer13-GFAP validated the mass spectrometry results in AxD patients.
source: Further, immunoblot analysis using a phospho-specific antibody (KT13) (Sekimata et al., 1996) against pSer13-GFAP validated the mass spectrometry results in the AxD patients (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: pSer13-GFAP is primarily associated with the more aggressive, infantile form of AxD.
source: Although there was one notable outlier in each age group (Figure 2B lanes 3 and 11), our results suggest that pSer13-GFAP is primarily associated with the more aggressive, infantile form of AxD.
evidence: This is an inference from the mass spectrometry and western blot data comparing young and old patients.

claim: The differences in pSer13-GFAP phosphorylation were not a result of age.
source: Furthermore, the differences in phosphorylation were not a result of age, since pSer13 GFAP was generally not present in the brain lysates from non-AxD control subjects, regardless of age (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from age-matched controls shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The S13D and S13E phospho-mimic mutants of GFAP assembled primarily into large aggregates, similar to the R79H AxD mutant.
source: Compared to wild-type (WT) GFAP, the S13D and S13E mutants assembled primarily into large aggregates, similar to the most common AxD-associated mutant R79H-GFAP (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification in Figure 3A-B.

claim: S13A GFAP formed mostly filaments, although they appeared shorter compared to WT GFAP.
source: S13A formed mostly filaments, although they appeared shorter compared to WT GFAP.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 3A.

claim: The S13A mutant formed abnormally short filaments in vitro.
source: Consistent with the phenotype observed in the transfected cells, the S13A mutant formed abnormally short filaments in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy of in vitro assembled GFAP shown in Figure 3C.

claim: S13D GFAP was completely incapable of filament assembly in vitro, forming globular structures that were homogeneous in size and not aggregation-prone.
source: In contrast, S13D was completely incapable of filament assembly, forming globular structures that were homogeneous in size and not aggregation-prone.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy of in vitro assembled GFAP shown in Figure 3C.

claim: S13 is a key site that regulates the assembly properties of GFAP.
source: Our results with the phospho-deficient and phospho-mimic mutants reveal that S13 is a key site that regulates the assembly properties of GFAP and that its phosphorylation status may modulate the dynamics between filaments and aggregates.
evidence: This is an inference from the in vitro and cell-based assembly data for S13 mutants.

claim: The phosphorylation status of S13 may modulate the dynamics between filaments and aggregates.
source: Our results with the phospho-deficient and phospho-mimic mutants reveal that S13 is a key site that regulates the assembly properties of GFAP and that its phosphorylation status may modulate the dynamics between filaments and aggregates.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed effects of S13 mutations on GFAP assembly.

claim: iPSCs were generated using fibroblasts from a young AxD patient.
source: We generated iPSCs using fibroblasts from a young AxD patient and characterized their pluripotency by immunofluorescence staining (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the characterization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Karyotype analysis showed that there were no chromosomal abnormalities due to the reprogramming process.
source: Karyotype analysis showed that there were no chromosomal abnormalities due to the reprogramming process (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by karyotype data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Isogenic control cells were generated by correcting the heterozygous point mutation in GFAP (c.715C > T, p.R239C) using CRISPR/Cas9 mediated gene editing.
source: To generate isogenic control cells, we corrected the heterozygous point mutation in GFAP (c.715C > T, p.R239C) using CRISPR/Cas9 mediated gene editing (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: There were no off-target effects due to the CRISPR editing procedure.
source: We confirmed that there were no off-target effects due to the editing procedure (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated based on off-target analysis data.

claim: GFAP levels were significantly higher in iPSC-astrocytes that carried the heterozygous GFAP point mutation relative to isogenic controls.
source: To assess if our model recapitulated key features of AxD, we analyzed total GFAP expression in the iPSC-astrocytes by immunoblot, and found that GFAP levels were significantly higher in the cells that carried the heterozygous GFAP point mutation (AxD patient and CRISPR control lines) relative to the isogenic controls (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantification shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Elevated GFAP levels in AxD iPSC-astrocytes is consistent with in vivo observations of GFAP levels in AxD patients.
source: This is consistent with in vivo observations of GFAP levels in AxD patients (Jany et al., 2015) and mouse models (Jany et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: High-molecular-mass (hmm) GFAP oligomers were present in the AxD iPSC-astrocytes.
source: In addition, high-molecular-mass (hmm) GFAP oligomers were present in the AxD iPSC-astrocytes, similar to what we observed when we ectopically expressed the R239C-GFAP mutant (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: AxD mutant iPSC-astrocytes formed both GFAP filaments and perinuclear aggregates.
source: Finally, we observed by immunofluorescence staining that the AxD mutant iPSC-astrocytes formed both GFAP filaments and perinuclear aggregates (Figure 5B), whereas the isogenic control iPSC-astrocytes formed only GFAP filaments (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Isogenic control iPSC-astrocytes formed only GFAP filaments.
source: Finally, we observed by immunofluorescence staining that the AxD mutant iPSC-astrocytes formed both GFAP filaments and perinuclear aggregates (Figure 5B), whereas the isogenic control iPSC-astrocytes formed only GFAP filaments (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In vivo, GFAP antibodies stain the periphery, while DAPI stains the core of RFs.
source: In vivo, GFAP antibodies stain the periphery, while DAPI stains the core of RFs (Der Perng et al., 2006; Sosunov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: In vitro-derived AxD iPSC-astrocytes displayed RF-like perinuclear aggregates staining positively for GFAP at their periphery and DAPI in the center.
source: The in vitro-derived AxD iPSC-astrocytes displayed similar characteristics, with RF-like perinuclear aggregates staining positively for GFAP at their periphery and DAPI in the center (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 5B.

claim: pSer13-GFAP signal was detected strongly within the core of the perinuclear GFAP aggregates of AxD iPSC-astrocytes.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, pSer13-GFAP signal was detected strongly within the core of the perinuclear GFAP aggregates of AxD iPSC-astrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 6A.

claim: pSer13-GFAP signal was observed in isogenic control cells.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, we also observed pSer13-GFAP signal in the isogenic control cells, possibly triggered by the in vitro culture conditions.
evidence: This is stated based on immunofluorescence observations in Figure 6A.

claim: In isogenic control astrocytes, pSer13-GFAP organization was filamentous and paralleled that of total GFAP.
source: Nevertheless, unlike AxD astrocytes, in the isogenic control astrocytes pSer13-GFAP organization was filamentous and paralleled that of total GFAP.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Only in the presence of the AxD disease mutation, pSer13-GFAP is incorporated within the core of perinuclear inclusions.
source: Therefore, the in vitro iPSC-astrocyte model revealed that, only in the presence of the AxD disease mutation, pSer13-GFAP is incorporated within the core of perinuclear inclusions.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of AxD and isogenic control astrocytes in Figure 6A.

claim: The pSer13-positive GFAP aggregates appeared adjacent to prominent nuclear invaginations.
source: Furthermore, the pSer13-positive GFAP aggregates appeared adjacent to prominent nuclear invaginations (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Nuclear deformations similar to those observed in AxD iPSC-astrocytes are present in RF-bearing astrocytes in AxD human brain.
source: Nuclear deformations, similar to what we observed in the AxD iPSC-astrocytes, are also present in RF-bearing astrocytes in AxD human brain (Sosunov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: Filamentous bundles were observed on the cytoplasmic side of the nuclear invaginations in AxD iPSC-astrocytes.
source: While we observed filamentous bundles on the cytoplasmic side of the nuclear invaginations, the nuclear envelope appeared intact (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy imaging shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The nuclear envelope appeared intact in AxD iPSC-astrocytes with nuclear invaginations.
source: While we observed filamentous bundles on the cytoplasmic side of the nuclear invaginations, the nuclear envelope appeared intact (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy imaging shown in Figure 6B.

claim: pSer13-GFAP marks cytoplasmic GFAP aggregates adjacent to nuclear invaginations.
source: Thus, pSer13-GFAP marks cytoplasmic GFAP aggregates adjacent to nuclear invaginations.
evidence: This is an inference from the immunofluorescence and electron microscopy data.

claim: An increase in high-molecular-mass ~100 kDa GFAP oligomer was observed in the phospho-mimic mutant S13D.
source: In line with our immunofluorescence result (Figure 3A), we observed an increase in high-molecular-mass ~100 kDa GFAP oligomer in the phospho-mimic mutant by immunoblot analysis (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Increased levels of a cleaved GFAP fragment (24 kDa) were observed in S13D and S13E, which was significantly lower in WT- and S13A-GFAP.
source: However, more strikingly, we observed increased levels of a cleaved GFAP fragment (24 kDa) in S13D and S13E, which was significantly lower in WT- and S13A-GFAP (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and quantification shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Cleavage of GFAP by caspase-6 in vitro generates two fragments of 24 and 26 kDa size.
source: Cleavage of GFAP by caspase-6 in vitro generates two fragments of 24 and 26 kDa size (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: The 24 kDa C-terminal fragment of GFAP is recognized by the monoclonal GA5 antibody.
source: The 24 kDa C-terminal fragment is recognized by the monoclonal GA5 antibody, (Chen et al., 2013) which was used here.
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: A peptide inhibitor of caspase-6 (Ac-VEID-CHO) significantly reduced the amount of cleaved S13D-GFAP.
source: Therefore, we tested the effect of a peptide inhibitor of caspase-6 (Ac-VEID-CHO), and found that it significantly reduced the amount of cleaved S13D-GFAP (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and quantification shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: Augmented cleavage of S13D-GFAP was observed when combined with an AxD-causing mutation (S13D/R79H double mutant).
source: Furthermore, we observed augmented cleavage of S13D-GFAP when combined with an AxD-causing mutation (S13D/R79H double mutant), and this was also blocked by the caspase-6 inhibitor (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and quantification shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: Cleavage of S13D/R79H double mutant GFAP was blocked by the caspase-6 inhibitor.
source: Furthermore, we observed augmented cleavage of S13D-GFAP when combined with an AxD-causing mutation (S13D/R79H double mutant), and this was also blocked by the caspase-6 inhibitor (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and quantification shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: R79H GFAP showed phosphorylation at S13, Y14, S16, and S17.
source: Further analysis of the AxD mutant R79H in the transfection system revealed phosphorylation not only at S13, but also at nearby Y14, S16, and S17 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by 2D gel and mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutagenesis of S16 and S17 to non-phosphorylatable alanines reduced both the cleavage and oligomerization of R79H GFAP.
source: Of note, mutagenesis of S16 and S17 to non-phosphorylatable alanines reduced both the cleavage and oligomerization of R79H (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: S13, S16 and S17 are part of a segment in the GFAP head domain that is a potential target for several kinases.
source: Phospho-motif analysis revealed that S13, S16 and S17 are part of a segment in the GFAP head domain that is a potential target for several kinases (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on computational phospho-motif analysis.

claim: Candidate kinases for phosphorylating S13, S16, and S17 include casein kinase 2 (CK2), protein kinase A (PKA), PKC, MAP kinase activated protein kinase 2 (MAPKAP2), and glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3).
source: Candidate kinases include casein kinase 2 (CK2), protein kinase A (PKA), PKC, MAP kinase activated protein kinase 2 (MAPKAP2), and glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3).
evidence: This is based on computational phospho-motif analysis.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser13 (and nearby S16/17) may promote caspase-6-mediated cleavage of GFAP in the context of AxD mutations.
source: These data suggest that phosphorylation of Ser13 (and nearby S16/17) may promote caspase-6-mediated cleavage of GFAP in the context of AxD mutations.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed correlation between phosphorylation and cleavage.

claim: Increased levels of cleaved GFAP were observed in AxD iPSC-astrocytes compared to isogenic control astrocytes.
source: In line with that, we observed increased levels of cleaved GFAP (upon normalization for total GFAP) in the AxD iPSC-astrocytes compared to isogenic control astrocytes (Figure 7E), along with intense caspase-6 staining within perinuclear GFAP aggregates in AxD iPSC-astrocytes, but not isogenic control astrocytes (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Intense caspase-6 staining was observed within perinuclear GFAP aggregates in AxD iPSC-astrocytes, but not isogenic control astrocytes.
source: In line with that, we observed increased levels of cleaved GFAP (upon normalization for total GFAP) in the AxD iPSC-astrocytes compared to isogenic control astrocytes (Figure 7E), along with intense caspase-6 staining within perinuclear GFAP aggregates in AxD iPSC-astrocytes, but not isogenic control astrocytes (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The D225E mutation reduced cleavage of S13D GFAP by >90%.
source: As shown in Figure 8A–B, the D225E mutation reduced cleavage of S13D GFAP by >90%.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and quantification shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: The D225E mutation resulted in partial rescue of filament structure in S13D.
source: This resulted in partial rescue of filament structure in S13D, although the D225E mutation on its own caused significant filament bundling and perinuclear structures that resembled large aggregates (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: The D225E mutation on its own caused significant filament bundling and perinuclear structures that resembled large aggregates.
source: This resulted in partial rescue of filament structure in S13D, although the D225E mutation on its own caused significant filament bundling and perinuclear structures that resembled large aggregates (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: The caspase-6 inhibitor Ac-VEID-CHO reduced both the size of the S13D aggregates and the presence of ~100 kDa hmm GFAP oligomers.
source: We also tested the effect of the caspase-6 inhibitor Ac-VEID-CHO, and found that it reduced both the size of the S13D aggregates (Figure 8E) and the presence of ~100 kDa hmm GFAP oligomers (Figure 8F–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figure 8E-G.

claim: Filament bundles were observed in WT and S13D GFAP treated with Ac-VEID-CHO.
source: However, similar to the mutagenesis experiment, filament bundles were observed in WT and S13D GFAP treated with Ac-VEID-CHO, suggesting that caspase-6 regulates both aggregation and normal GFAP filament re-organization.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Caspase-6 regulates both aggregation and normal GFAP filament re-organization.
source: However, similar to the mutagenesis experiment, filament bundles were observed in WT and S13D GFAP treated with Ac-VEID-CHO, suggesting that caspase-6 regulates both aggregation and normal GFAP filament re-organization.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed effects of caspase-6 inhibition.

claim: Caspase-6 is expressed in the brain tissue from all 8 AxD patients who died very young.
source: Using immunoblot analysis of total brain lysates, we found that caspase-6 is expressed in the brain tissue from all 8 AxD patients who died very young, but is essentially undetectable in the patients who survived longer (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Caspase-6 is essentially undetectable in AxD patients who survived longer.
source: Using immunoblot analysis of total brain lysates, we found that caspase-6 is expressed in the brain tissue from all 8 AxD patients who died very young, but is essentially undetectable in the patients who survived longer (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: There was a significant increase in caspase-6 expression selectively in young AxD patients, but not in age-matched controls or older AxD patients.
source: To ensure caspase-6 expression is not simply more abundant in young individuals, we compared brain lysates from young and old AxD patients to non-AxD control brains from age-matched individuals, and observed a significant increase in caspase-6 expression selectively in young AxD patients, but not in the other groups (Figure 9B–C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and quantification shown in Figure 9B-C.

claim: Cleaved GFAP was detected in extracts from AxD patient brains.
source: To determine the extent of caspase-6-cleaved GFAP in AxD patient brains, we utilized an antibody that specifically recognizes N-terminally caspase-6-cleaved GFAP (D225) (Chen et al., 2013). We detected cleaved GFAP in extracts from AxD patient brains, and we observed a significant increase in the amount of D225 signal in young AxD patients, which paralleled the increased pSer13 signal in these samples (Figure 9D–E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: A significant increase in the amount of cleaved GFAP (D225 signal) was observed in young AxD patients, which paralleled the increased pSer13 signal.
source: We detected cleaved GFAP in extracts from AxD patient brains, and we observed a significant increase in the amount of D225 signal in young AxD patients, which paralleled the increased pSer13 signal in these samples (Figure 9D–E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and quantification shown in Figure 9D-E.

claim: Brain tissues from young AxD patients stained intensely for cleaved GFAP, while the signal was significantly weaker in AxD patients who were older.
source: In agreement with the biochemical evidence, brain tissues from young AxD patients stained intensely for cleaved GFAP, while the signal was significantly weaker in AxD patients who were older (Figure 9F; Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 9F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cleaved GFAP signal was particularly strong around perinuclear areas and surrounded circular structures that stained positive for DAPI in young AxD patient brain tissue.
source: The signal was particularly strong around perinuclear areas and surrounded circular structures that stained positive for DAPI (Figure 9F, bottom panels), similar to what we observed in the AxD iPSC-astrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Caspase-6 expression in AxD patient brain tissue parallels the presence of cleaved GFAP.
source: Thus, our results show that caspase-6 expression in AxD patient brain tissue parallels the presence of cleaved GFAP, and both are selectively and significantly elevated in patients who succumbed to the disease very early in life.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation observed between caspase-6 and cleaved GFAP in patient samples.

claim: Caspase-6 and cleaved GFAP are both selectively and significantly elevated in AxD patients who succumbed to the disease very early in life.
source: Thus, our results show that caspase-6 expression in AxD patient brain tissue parallels the presence of cleaved GFAP, and both are selectively and significantly elevated in patients who succumbed to the disease very early in life.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot and immunofluorescence data from patient samples.

claim: Missense mutations affecting discrete domains on the GFAP molecule share a common PTM signature associated with compromised GFAP proteostasis in severe AxD.
source: Our study reveals that missense mutations, affecting discrete domains on the GFAP molecule, share a common PTM signature that is associated with compromised GFAP proteostasis in the severe form of AxD.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Head domain phosphorylation promotes defective filament assembly and perinuclear accumulation of mutant GFAP.
source: Using patient brain tissue and human iPSC-derived AxD astrocytes, we show that head domain phosphorylation promotes defective filament assembly and perinuclear accumulation and incorporation of mutant GFAP within nuclear invaginations.
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro assembly data (Figure 3C) and iPSC-astrocyte imaging (Figure 6A).

claim: Head domain phosphorylation promotes incorporation of mutant GFAP within nuclear invaginations.
source: Using patient brain tissue and human iPSC-derived AxD astrocytes, we show that head domain phosphorylation promotes defective filament assembly and perinuclear accumulation and incorporation of mutant GFAP within nuclear invaginations.
evidence: This is supported by the iPSC-astrocyte imaging showing pSer13-GFAP in aggregates near nuclear invaginations (Figure 6A-B).

claim: Phospho-mimetic mutation S13D completely abolished the ability of GFAP to form filaments in vitro.
source: Phospho-mimetic mutation S13D completely abolished the ability of GFAP to form filaments in vitro, without leading to aggregation.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy of in vitro assembled GFAP shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Phospho-mimic S13D-and S13E-GFAP mutants formed highly abnormal perinuclear aggregates in transfected SW13vim- cells.
source: In transfected SW13vim- cells, phospho mimic S13D-and S13E-GFAP mutants formed highly abnormal perinuclear aggregates that correlated with increased cleavage of GFAP by caspase-6.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 3A) and western blot data (Figure 7A-B).

claim: Phospho-mimic S13D-and S13E-GFAP mutants showed increased cleavage of GFAP by caspase-6 in transfected cells.
source: In transfected SW13vim- cells, phospho mimic S13D-and S13E-GFAP mutants formed highly abnormal perinuclear aggregates that correlated with increased cleavage of GFAP by caspase-6.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing increased cleaved GFAP in S13D and S13E mutants (Figure 7A-B).

claim: A dramatic increase in caspase-6 expression was detected in the brain tissue of AxD patients who succumbed to the disease very early in life.
source: We detected a dramatic increase in caspase-6 expression, in association with Ser13 phosphorylation and cleavage of GFAP, in the brain tissue of AxD patients who succumbed to the disease very early in life.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from patient brain tissue (Figure 9A-C).

claim: The N-terminal caspase-6 fragment of GFAP promotes filament aggregation in vitro.
source: While the N-terminal caspase-6 fragment of GFAP promotes filament aggregation in vitro (Chen et al., 2013), presently we do not have direct evidence of cause and effect between caspase-6 cleavage and GFAP aggregation in AxD patient cells.
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: There is no direct evidence of cause and effect between caspase-6 cleavage and GFAP aggregation in AxD patient cells.
source: While the N-terminal caspase-6 fragment of GFAP promotes filament aggregation in vitro (Chen et al., 2013), presently we do not have direct evidence of cause and effect between caspase-6 cleavage and GFAP aggregation in AxD patient cells.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of a limitation in the current study.

claim: Caspase-6 is not expressed highly in the normal human brain, especially after birth.
source: Caspase-6 is not expressed highly in the normal human brain, especially after birth (Godefroy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: AxD mutations promote activation and nuclear accumulation of p53.
source: This is supported by previous studies showing that AxD mutations promote activation and nuclear accumulation of p53 (Wang et al., 2015), which can directly induce caspase-6 expression (MacLachlan and El-Deiry, 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: p53 can directly induce caspase-6 expression.
source: This is supported by previous studies showing that AxD mutations promote activation and nuclear accumulation of p53 (Wang et al., 2015), which can directly induce caspase-6 expression (MacLachlan and El-Deiry, 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: Monitoring the levels of pSer13-GFAP (in addition to total GFAP) in AxD patient cerebrospinal fluid or blood may provide added sensitivity for disease activity.
source: Given our findings that pSer13-GFAP is enriched in the most aggressive form of AxD, monitoring the levels of this phospho-epitope (in addition to total GFAP) in AxD patient cerebrospinal fluid or blood may provide added sensitivity for disease activity (Jany et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about potential clinical applications based on the study findings.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser13 by protein kinase C and cAMP-dependent protein kinase was initially described in vitro using purified recombinant GFAP.
source: Phosphorylation of Ser13 by protein kinase C and cAMP-dependent protein kinase was initially described in vitro using purified recombinant GFAP (Inagaki et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: In the presence of active kinases, Ser-13 phosphorylation occurred in conjunction with phosphorylation at three additional sites (Thr-7, Ser-8, and Ser-34).
source: In the presence of active kinases, Ser-13 phosphorylation occurred in conjunction with phosphorylation at three additional sites (Thr-7, Ser-8, and Ser-34).
evidence: This is stated based on previous in vitro studies.

claim: Phosphorylation of monomeric GFAP at Ser13, Thr-7, Ser-8, and Ser-34 prevented filament assembly.
source: Phosphorylation of monomeric GFAP at these sites prevented filament assembly, while phosphorylation of in vitro assembled GFAP filaments led to their disassembly (Inagaki et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: Phosphorylation of in vitro assembled GFAP filaments at Ser13, Thr-7, Ser-8, and Ser-34 led to their disassembly.
source: Phosphorylation of monomeric GFAP at these sites prevented filament assembly, while phosphorylation of in vitro assembled GFAP filaments led to their disassembly (Inagaki et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: Aurora-B and Rho-associated kinase phosphorylate GFAP in cultured astrocytoma cells during mitosis.
source: Using the same antibody to pSer13-GFAP that we used in this paper (clone KT13) it was later shown that Aurora-B and Rho-associated kinase phosphorylate GFAP in cultured astrocytoma cells during mitosis (Inagaki et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: Human and mouse AxD astrocytes with RFs display mitotic abnormalities.
source: This may bear relevance to AxD, since human and mouse AxD astrocytes with RFs display mitotic abnormalities (Sosunov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: In vivo, the distribution of pSer13 localization was not limited to mitotic astrocytes in knock-in mice with the human GFAP head domain.
source: However, it was also shown using knock-in mice with the human GFAP head domain that, in vivo, the distribution of pSer13 localization was not limited to mitotic astrocytes, but that select astrocyte populations within multiple regions were pSer13 positive, such as those in the olfactory bulb, subpial regions, and subventricular zone (Takemura et al., 2002b; Hagemann et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: The regional distribution of pSer13 largely overlaps with areas that are known to be most enriched in RFs in the AxD mouse model.
source: Interestingly, the regional distribution of pSer13 largely overlaps with areas that are known to be most enriched in RFs in the AxD mouse model (Hagemann et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: Caspase-mediated proteolysis of IF proteins is an important mechanism by which the filament networks re-organize during apoptosis.
source: Caspase-mediated proteolysis of IF proteins is an important mechanism by which the filament networks re-organize during apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Caspase-6 is frequently implicated in cleavage of IF proteins at a conserved motif within the linker L12 region of the rod domain.
source: Although multiple effector caspases are capable of cleaving IF proteins, caspase-6 is frequently implicated in cleavage at a conserved motif within the linker L12 region of the rod domain, which results in the generation of two fragments of similar sizes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with subsequent citations.

claim: Caspase-6 cleavage of type I keratins was initially demonstrated.
source: This was initially demonstrated to be the case for the type I keratins (Caulín et al., 1997), and later shown to also occur on vimentin (Byun et al., 2001), desmin (Chen et al., 2003), A-type lamins (Ruchaud et al., 2002), and GFAP (Hol and Pekny, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: Caspase-6 cleavage also occurs on vimentin, desmin, A-type lamins, and GFAP.
source: This was initially demonstrated to be the case for the type I keratins (Caulín et al., 1997), and later shown to also occur on vimentin (Byun et al., 2001), desmin (Chen et al., 2003), A-type lamins (Ruchaud et al., 2002), and GFAP (Hol and Pekny, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: The N-terminal fragment of caspase-6 cleaved GFAP directly impairs assembly of full-length GFAP and promotes aggregation in vitro.
source: The N-terminal fragment directly impairs assembly of full-length GFAP and promotes aggregation in vitro (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: GFAP cleavage is significantly increased in AxD tissues from patients presenting with an aggressive form of AxD.
source: Using a specific antibody recognizing the N-terminal GFAP fragment (D225), we show here that GFAP cleavage is significantly increased in AxD tissues from patients presenting with an aggressive form of AxD, and that this parallels elevated expression of caspase-6.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data from patient tissue (Figure 9D-F).

claim: Inhibition of caspase-6 or mutagenesis of the cleavage site on GFAP cannot fully resolve aggregate formation in cells.
source: However, we were not able to demonstrate in cells that inhibition of caspase-6, or mutagenesis of the cleavage site on GFAP, can resolve aggregate formation.
evidence: This is stated based on the experimental results shown in Figure 8.

claim: Caspase-6 has a more complex function, likely involving cytoskeletal remodeling in response to stress.
source: These results point to a more complex function for caspase-6, likely involving cytoskeletal remodeling in response to stress.
evidence: This is speculation based on the inability to fully rescue aggregation by blocking caspase-6.

claim: Caspase-6 upregulation has been reported in other neurodegenerative diseases involving protein aggregation, including Huntington's Disease (HD) and Alzheimer's Disease (AD).
source: Indeed, caspase-6 upregulation has been reported in other neurodegenerative diseases involving protein aggregation, including Huntington's Disease (HD) and Alzheimer's Disease (AD) (Albrecht et al., 2007; Graham et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a caspase-6 cleavage site on the aggregation-prone proteins in both AD (amyloid precursor protein) and HD (huntingtin).
source: Similar to GFAP, there is a caspase-6 cleavage site on the aggregation-prone proteins in both AD (amyloid precursor protein) and HD (huntingtin).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In caspase-6 cleavage-resistant genetic mouse models of both HD and AD, neuronal dysfunction and degeneration are rescued.
source: Furthermore, in caspase-6 cleavage-resistant genetic mouse models of both HD and AD, neuronal dysfunction and degeneration are rescued (Graham et al., 2006; Galvan et al., 2006; Saganich et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Caspase-6 can promote neurodegeneration via induction of neuronal apoptosis or axon pruning.
source: Caspase-6 can promote neurodegeneration via induction of neuronal apoptosis or axon pruning (Geden et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: The functions of caspase-6 in astrocytes are not clear.
source: However, the functions of caspase-6 in astrocytes are not clear.
evidence: This is an explicit statement of a knowledge gap.

claim: Caspase-6 localizes within the perinuclear GFAP inclusions in AxD iPSC-astrocytes.
source: Based on our demonstration that caspase-6 localizes within the perinuclear GFAP inclusions in the AxD iPSC-astrocytes, it is intriguing to speculate that, similar to keratin inclusions in epithelial cells (Dinsdale et al., 2004), RFs sequester active caspases away from other cellular substrates and may protect reactive astrocytes from apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: RFs may sequester active caspases away from other cellular substrates and protect reactive astrocytes from apoptosis.
source: Based on our demonstration that caspase-6 localizes within the perinuclear GFAP inclusions in the AxD iPSC-astrocytes, it is intriguing to speculate that, similar to keratin inclusions in epithelial cells (Dinsdale et al., 2004), RFs sequester active caspases away from other cellular substrates and may protect reactive astrocytes from apoptosis.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to keratin inclusions and the observed localization of caspase-6.

claim: AxD astrocytes have defects in the secretory pathway, impaired ATP release, and attenuated calcium waves.
source: For example, these novel tools have revealed that AxD astrocytes have defects in the secretory pathway, impaired ATP release, and attenuated calcium waves (Jones et al., 2018); that they inhibit oligodendrocyte precursor cell proliferation (Li et al., 2018), providing a potential mechanistic explanation for the degeneration of white matter observed in patients; and that they have defects in mechanotransduction signaling pathways (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: AxD astrocytes inhibit oligodendrocyte precursor cell proliferation.
source: For example, these novel tools have revealed that AxD astrocytes have defects in the secretory pathway, impaired ATP release, and attenuated calcium waves (Jones et al., 2018); that they inhibit oligodendrocyte precursor cell proliferation (Li et al., 2018), providing a potential mechanistic explanation for the degeneration of white matter observed in patients; and that they have defects in mechanotransduction signaling pathways (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: AxD astrocytes have defects in mechanotransduction signaling pathways.
source: For example, these novel tools have revealed that AxD astrocytes have defects in the secretory pathway, impaired ATP release, and attenuated calcium waves (Jones et al., 2018); that they inhibit oligodendrocyte precursor cell proliferation (Li et al., 2018), providing a potential mechanistic explanation for the degeneration of white matter observed in patients; and that they have defects in mechanotransduction signaling pathways (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: The perinuclear accumulation of pSer13-GFAP in AxD iPSC-astrocytes was associated with prominent nuclear abnormalities.
source: A novel aspect of the AxD astrocyte cell model that we generated in our study is the perinuclear accumulation of pSer13-GFAP that was associated with prominent nuclear abnormalities.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and electron microscopy data (Figure 6A-B).

claim: Patient-derived iPSC-astrocytes replicate a key phenotypic characteristic of RF-bearing AxD astrocytes in vivo, since nuclear invaginations have been described in electron microscopy studies of AxD mouse models and AxD patient cortex.
source: As such, these patient-derived cells replicate a key phenotypic characteristic of RF-bearing AxD astrocytes in vivo, since nuclear invaginations have been described in electron microscopy studies of AxD mouse models and AxD patient cortex (Sosunov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: DAPI is a reliable and sensitive marker of RFs in human and mouse brain.
source: Another important parallel is that the GFAP inclusions we observe in the AxD patient astrocytes in vitro stain positive for DAPI, and it was shown that DAPI is a reliable and sensitive marker of RFs in human and mouse brain (Sosunov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: Patient-derived iPSC-astrocytes provide a unique model system to investigate cytoplasmic-nuclear mechanics in AxD.
source: Therefore patient-derived iPSC-astrocytes provide a unique model system to investigate cytoplasmic-nuclear mechanics in AxD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed nuclear invaginations in the iPSC-astrocyte model.

claim: Invaginations of the nucleus have been described in physiological and pathological states.
source: Invaginations of the nucleus, such as those we observe here, have been described in physiological and pathological states (Malhas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a review article.

claim: Control of nuclear shape is critical for regulation of gene expression and response to mechanotransduction signals.
source: Control of nuclear shape is critical for regulation of gene expression and response to mechanotransduction signals (Uhler and Shivashankar, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a review article.

claim: Mutations in lamin A lead to defective nuclear morphology in Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS), where patients experience accelerated aging.
source: The effects of impaired nuclear morphology can be very severe, as evidenced by mutations in lamin A that lead to defective nuclear morphology in Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS), where patients experience accelerated aging (Eriksson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: There is a direct link between intermediate filaments, actin and the nuclear envelope within nuclear invaginations.
source: An elegant study combining multiple 3D imaging strategies established a direct link between intermediate filaments, actin and the nuclear envelope within nuclear invaginations, and genetic evidence indicates that filamentous actin may play a role in generating these structures (Jorgens et al., 2017; Frost et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Filamentous actin may play a role in generating nuclear invaginations.
source: An elegant study combining multiple 3D imaging strategies established a direct link between intermediate filaments, actin and the nuclear envelope within nuclear invaginations, and genetic evidence indicates that filamentous actin may play a role in generating these structures (Jorgens et al., 2017; Frost et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Nuclear invaginations are hypothesized to provide localized control of gene expression and nuclear-cytoplasmic transport deep within the nucleus.
source: It is hypothesized that nuclear invaginations provide localized control of gene expression and nuclear-cytoplasmic transport deep within the nucleus, since they have been found to contain calcium receptors and nuclear pores (Malhas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a review article.

claim: Nuclear invaginations have been found to contain calcium receptors and nuclear pores.
source: It is hypothesized that nuclear invaginations provide localized control of gene expression and nuclear-cytoplasmic transport deep within the nucleus, since they have been found to contain calcium receptors and nuclear pores (Malhas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a review article.

claim: This study provides the first link between abnormal cytoplasmic PTM processing and perinuclear accumulation of mutant GFAP with nuclear defects.
source: Our study provides the first link between abnormal cytoplasmic PTM processing and perinuclear accumulation of mutant GFAP with nuclear defects, setting the stage to address how nucleo-cytoskeletal coupling is adversely impacted by defective IF proteostasis in AxD and related human diseases.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contribution.
